slides.title: Four things to start with.
slides.text: Create, read, update and delete are the four broad kinds of operations from the last chapter. A policy gives a role some of them on one piece of data. Never a person directly: always a role, or, for your own agents, the agent itself (Identity chapter). Only the owner writes policies.
slides.deep: A policy is a signed certificate: role, data, list of operations, conditions, expiry, plus the proof chain back to the seal. Only the owner writes them, through its own agents (D54). Conditions come later in this chapter, proofs in Checking, expiry in Endings.

slides.title: Mia, Alice and Bob get the list.
slides.text: You make a role “household”, give it read, create and update on the list, and add Mia, Alice and Bob. They can see the list, add things and tick them off. They can't delete it, and they can't write policies.
slides.deep: Mia, Alice and Bob are added to the role “household”. Technically: the owner signs a new role record (theos/role@1) with them in it and wraps the role key for each one's identity key (both explained in the Keys chapter). The data's policies don't change at all.

slides.title: The plumber gets one item.
slides.text: “Fix the tap” is its own little piece of data, linked from the list. Born inside the list, it starts with the list's policies. You add one more: the role “plumber” may read and update this item, and nothing else.
slides.deep: Read opens a whole piece of data, because the data key does. So an item shared on its own is its own piece of data, with its own data key and its own schema (a to-do item), linked from the list. New data born inside the list copies the list's policies once, at birth.

slides.title: Every policy is one sentence.
slides.text: A policy says: this role may perform these operations, on this data, until a date: its {expiry}. Nothing more. Everything anyone may ever do with your data is written in policies like this one.
slides.deep: A policy is a signed certificate with one shape everywhere: who (a role), on what (this data), operations (each optionally narrowed by at, where or a limit), expiry, and a proof chain back to the seal. An identity's own policies use the same shape (Identity chapter). People see “policy”; underneath it is a capability.

slides.title: What a policy can allow.
slides.text: Each operation is one thing a role may do. Four are about the content. Want, keep and sync are about carrying data; they come in the Carriers chapter.
list: Each covers its engine operations: read covers get, find, search and the other ways of looking (Operations chapter).
Writing and ending policies is not on the list: that is what owning means.
slides.deep: The full list: create, read, update, delete, want, keep, sync. Each covers its specific engine operations (D53). Writing and ending policies is no operation anyone can be given; it belongs to the owner (D30, D54).

slides.title: Every operation looks the same.
slides.text: Every operation is written the same way, in every policy and in the engine: what, at which path, and optionally which entries and how many. Read too: read what? “at” answers it. An empty path, "", means the whole thing.
slides.deep: One shape, one schema (D56): operation, at (a JSON Pointer), where, limit; never a bare name. A policy names broad operations; the engine's operation record (theos/operation@1, Operations chapter) uses the same fields with a specific operation and its own inputs. An engine operation is allowed when a policy entry covers its broad operation, its path lies under at, and where and limit hold.

slides.title: Conditions make a policy narrower.
slides.text: Each operation can carry {conditions}: only entries that match, only so many times. Like the path, they can only narrow.
slides.deep: Every operation uses the same conditions: at (a JSON Pointer prefix), where (matching entries, for example author = $self), limit. Changes are checked by every verifying peer. Read is checked by the reader's own engine: the data key opens the whole piece of data, so anything that must stay unseen has to be its own data (D55). Like Meadowcap's areas, each condition can only narrow.

slides.title: Owning means writing the policies.
slides.text: Owning is not an operation you give to someone. It is the one policy the seal signed at birth, and it does what no other policy can: write policies and end them, keep data longer, erase it, open its archive. The owner's agents do this for it, through the owner's own policies (Identity chapter).
slides.deep: Ownership acts belong to the owner alone (D30, D54): writing and ending policies, retain, erase and opening the archive. An agent performs them only if its identity policy gives it own over its owner (D46). Nobody else writes policies, and ownership is never handed over: whoever needs to work on the data gets a policy.

slides.title: Only the owner never expires.
slides.text: The policy the seal signed at birth names the owner. It has no expiry, so data can never end up with nobody allowed to look after it. Every other policy expires.
slides.deep: The genesis certificate has no expiry, and ownership does not move: there is no hand-over. Whoever else needs to work on the data gets a policy.

slides.title: Policies, in short.
list: A policy: this role may perform these operations, on this data, until then.
Every operation, read included, can be narrowed by conditions.
Only the owner writes and ends policies; its own policy never expires.
slides.deep: Policies are capabilities attached to roles, written by the owner alone, narrowable, expiring by default, ended by events, and checked offline by every peer.
